concepts.name: Smart Cities Mission: Genesis, Objectives and Core Philosophy
key_dimensions: Launch year (2015), nodal ministry (MoHUA), and distinction from earlier JNNURM
Twin objectives: retrofitting/redevelopment vs. greenfield development — UPSC trap on which is primary
Pan-City initiative vs. Area-Based Development (ABD) — scope and funding split
'Liveability, economic development, sustainability' triad as the definitional core

concepts.name: Selection Process: Challenge/Competition Method
key_dimensions: Two-stage competition: City Challenge Round 1 (state-level) and Round 2 (national-level) — frequently confused
Criteria for scoring: self-financing potential, citizen engagement score, past track record
Total cities selected: 100 cities across multiple rounds (2016–2018) — trap on exact number and phases
Distinction between 'shortlisted' vs. 'selected' cities and role of state governments in nomination

concepts.name: Funding Structure and Financial Architecture
key_dimensions: Central-State-ULB funding ratio: 50:50 (Centre:State+ULB) — trap on whether it is 50:25:25 or 50:50
Total outlay: ₹98,000 crore over 5 years (initially); per-city central allocation of ₹500 crore over 5 years
SPV's role in leveraging additional funds via PPP, bonds, user charges — not solely government-funded
Convergence with other schemes (AMRUT, PMAY-U, Swachh Bharat) for additional resource mobilization

concepts.name: Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV): Structure and Powers
key_dimensions: SPV as a limited company under Companies Act 2013 — not a statutory body, a key UPSC distinction
Shareholding: State Government and ULB hold 50:50 equity — Centre does NOT hold equity directly
SPV supersedes municipal corporation for project area — constitutional tension with 74th Amendment
CEO appointment, accountability to Board vs. elected municipal council — democratic deficit debate

concepts.name: Area-Based Development (ABD): Retrofitting, Redevelopment, and Greenfield
key_dimensions: Retrofitting: upgrading existing built-up area (>500 acres) with smart solutions — least disruptive
Redevelopment: replacement of existing built environment with higher FSI — most capital-intensive
Greenfield: new area development on vacant land (>250 acres) — GIFT City as prototype example
Each city must choose ONE primary ABD model — trap on whether multiple models are allowed simultaneously

concepts.name: Pan-City Smart Solutions: ICT and Technology Integration
key_dimensions: Pan-City applies city-wide (not just ABD area) — distinction from ABD is a frequent exam trap
At least one Pan-City solution mandatory per Smart City Proposal (SCP)
Focus areas: smart traffic management, e-governance, water/energy monitoring via sensors and IoT
Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC) as the technological nerve centre — its post-COVID adaptation

concepts.name: Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC): Role and Significance
key_dimensions: Real-time data aggregation from multiple city systems (traffic, utilities, emergency services)
COVID-19 repurposing of ICCCs for surveillance, quarantine monitoring, vaccine distribution — current affairs angle
Distinction between ICCC under SCM vs. similar control rooms under state police — jurisdictional overlap
Sustainability post-mission: operational cost challenge once central funding ends

concepts.name: Smart Cities Mission vs. AMRUT: Overlap, Distinction and Convergence
key_dimensions: SCM: 100 cities, area-based, competition-driven; AMRUT: 500 cities, city-wide, basic services focus
AMRUT focuses on water supply, sewerage, green spaces — SCM focuses on 'smart' solutions and ICT
Both under MoHUA but different funding, selection, and implementation mechanisms — classic UPSC trap
A city can be both a Smart City and an AMRUT city — overlap in selection lists

concepts.name: Smart Cities Mission vs. JNNURM: Evolution of Urban Mission Design
key_dimensions: JNNURM (2005): broader, input-based, reform-linked funding; SCM (2015): output/outcome-based, competitive
JNNURM covered 65 mission cities; SCM expanded to 100 — difference in targeting logic
SCM introduced SPV model absent in JNNURM — structural innovation
Both missions criticized for bypassing elected ULBs — continuity of democratic deficit concern

concepts.name: Citizen Participation and Demand-Driven Planning
key_dimensions: MyGov portal, mobile apps, and ward-level consultations as mandatory citizen engagement tools
Citizen engagement score as part of selection criteria — quantified participation, not just consultative
Critique: urban poor and informal sector underrepresented in digital engagement platforms
Smart City Advisory Forum (SCAF) at city level — composition (MP, MLA, Mayor, CEO) and advisory-only status

concepts.name: Smart City Advisory Forum (SCAF) and Governance Architecture
key_dimensions: SCAF: chaired by MP (Lok Sabha) of the city — trap on chairperson identity vs. SPV Board chairperson
Members include MLA, Mayor, CEO of SPV, representatives of civil society and industry
SCAF is advisory only — no executive/financial powers, unlike SPV which has full executive authority
Distinction between SCAF (advisory), SPV Board (executive), and Municipal Council (elected but sidelined)

concepts.name: 74th Constitutional Amendment and Smart Cities: Tension and Critique
key_dimensions: 12th Schedule functions (e.g., urban planning, regulation of land use) overlap with SPV's mandate
SPV operates in a defined area potentially bypassing elected ULB — violation of spirit of 74th Amendment
State governments nominate cities but SPV is state+ULB company — questions of democratic accountability
Reform vs. bypass debate: SCM as an incentive for ULB reform or as institutionalized bypassing of ULBs

concepts.name: Smart City Proposal (SCP): Components and Evaluation Framework
key_dimensions: SCP must include: city profile, vision, ABD proposal, Pan-City proposal, governance framework, financials
Innovation: cities that proposed self-financing models (PPP, value capture) scored higher
SCP evaluated on: boldness of vision, technical feasibility, financial sustainability, citizen support
Revision rounds allowed — cities that failed in Round 1 could resubmit (fast-track round)

concepts.name: PPP Model and Private Sector Role in Smart Cities
key_dimensions: SPV can enter PPP agreements — private developers, technology firms, utilities operators
Revenue models: user charges, advertisement revenue, naming rights, land monetization
Risk of privatization of urban services and exclusion of low-income groups — equity critique
Technology companies (IBM, Cisco, Siemens) as vendors — 'corporate smart city' critique vs. citizen-centric model

concepts.name: Smart Cities and Sustainable Development: Environmental Dimensions
key_dimensions: Green building norms, energy efficiency, renewable energy targets embedded in SCPs
Water recycling, rainwater harvesting, and smart metering as mandatory smart solution categories
SCM alignment with SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) — official government framing
Tension between greenfield development and loss of peri-urban agricultural/ecological land

concepts.name: Data Governance, Privacy and Surveillance Concerns in Smart Cities
key_dimensions: ICCCs collect real-time data on citizens — absence of a dedicated data protection law until DPDP Act 2023
CCTV networks, facial recognition, and mobility tracking — civil liberties vs. safety trade-off
Data ownership question: who owns city data — SPV, ULB, state government, or technology vendor?
Comparison with international models: Barcelona's citizen-data sovereignty vs. India's top-down data governance

concepts.name: Social Equity and Inclusion Deficit in Smart Cities
key_dimensions: ABD focus on select 'islands of excellence' — criticism of neglecting city-wide informal settlements
Displacement risk in redevelopment zones — informal traders, slum dwellers not adequately addressed
Digital divide: smart solutions presuppose smartphone/internet access, excluding urban poor
CAG and parliamentary committee reports flagging inclusion gaps — important for answer enrichment

concepts.name: Performance Assessment and Mission Extension
key_dimensions: Original mission period: 2015–2020; extended to 2023, then further to June 2024 — trap on current deadline
City-level monitoring via online dashboard (Smart Cities Dashboard/DataSmart Cities portal)
Completion metrics: projects tendered, awarded, completed — not just funds utilized
Ranking of Smart Cities: annual rankings by MoHUA (Ease of Living Index linkage) — assessment methodology

concepts.name: Lighthouse Cities and Global Benchmarking under SCM
key_dimensions: India's engagement with ISO 37120 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) standard for city indicators
Pune, Surat, Ahmedabad among early high-performers — used as case studies in UPSC answers
Global Smart City indices: IMD Smart City Index, Eden Strategy — India's comparative ranking
National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA) as knowledge partner for SCM — institutional support architecture

concepts.name: Post-Mission Sustainability: Institutionalization and Long-Term Viability
key_dimensions: What happens to SPV after mission ends — merger with ULB, continuation as company, or dissolution?
O&M (Operations & Maintenance) cost burden on ULBs which already have weak fiscal base
Technology obsolescence risk: smart infrastructure requires continuous upgrades unlike conventional infrastructure
Policy continuity question: SCM's future under new urban mission frameworks (National Urban Policy 2063 draft)
